    (∑ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), (antiFib k : ℝ)) = ((n : ℝ) ^ 3 + 5 * n + 6) / 6 := by
  have h := antiFib_sum_closed n
  have hcast : (6 : ℝ) * (∑ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), (antiFib k : ℝ))
      = (n : ℝ) ^ 3 + 5 * n + 6 := by
    have : ((6 * (∑ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), antiFib k) : ℕ) : ℝ)
        = ((n ^ 3 + 5 * n + 6 : ℕ) : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast congrArg (Nat.cast) h
    push_cast at this ⊢
    linarith [this]
  linarith [hcast]

antiderivative of the value-level density `antiFib n / n² → 1/2`.  (For exponential

theorem antiFib_cesaro :
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (∑ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), (antiFib k : ℝ)) / (n : ℝ) ^ 3)
      atTop (𝓝 (1 / 6)) := by
  have h1 : Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (1 : ℝ) / (n : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 0) :=

  have h2 : Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (1 : ℝ) / (n : ℝ) ^ 2) atTop (𝓝 0) := by

    simp only [mul_zero] at this

  have h3 : Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (1 : ℝ) / (n : ℝ) ^ 3) atTop (𝓝 0) := by

    simp only [mul_zero] at this
    convert this using 2 with n; ring
  have hev : ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,

    rw [antiFib_sum_real]; field_simp

# Future Directions — The Anti-Fibonacci Sequence

This cycle studied the addition-avoiding counterpart of the Fibonacci sequence:
the sequence beginning `1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22, …`, whose successive differences
are `0, 1, 2, 3, …` and whose closed form is `A(n) = 1 + n(n-1)/2`. Three exact
structural facts emerged: its partial sums obey the cubic identity
`6·(A(0)+···+A(n)) = n³ + 5n + 6`; a number `m` occurs in the sequence exactly when
`8m − 7` is a perfect square (equivalently, when `m − 1` is a triangular number); and
the cumulative sums grow with the finite cubic density `1/6`, the discrete
antiderivative of the value-level density `1/2`. The following conjectures grow
directly out of these findings.

## 1. A factorial tower of cumulative densities

Iterating the summation operator on the anti-Fibonacci sequence should produce a
clean staircase of constants: the values grow like `n²/2`, the first cumulative sums
like `n³/6`, the second like `n⁴/24`, and in general the `d`-fold cumulative sum
should be a polynomial of degree `d + 2` with leading coefficient `1/(d+2)!`.

The key insight is that repeated summation is a discrete antiderivative, so it should
promote the value density `1/2` through the factorials exactly the way iterated
integration turns `x²/2` into `x^(d+2)/(d+2)!`. Why now? The first two rungs of this
tower are now known exactly, which fixes both the pattern and the inductive step
needed to climb it, turning a numerical guess into a precise, provable recurrence.

## 2. Perfect-square membership as a fingerprint of quadratic growth

The discovery that the anti-Fibonacci values are exactly the integers `m` with
`8m − 7` a perfect square suggests a general principle: an integer sequence built by a
greedy additive-avoidance rule has a value-set of the form "the `m` for which some
fixed quadratic `Q(m)` is a perfect square" if and only if the sequence is eventually
a quadratic polynomial, and in that case `Q` is forced by the polynomial's
discriminant.

The key insight is that a perfect-square membership test is the arithmetic signature
of quadratic growth, because such a test makes the counting function grow like a
square-root, which in turn pins the sequence to degree two. Why now? We have a fully
worked instance of the phenomenon in hand, so both directions of the proposed
equivalence can be stress-tested on it before the general theory is attempted.

## 3. The avoided-sum shadow has density zero

Each anti-Fibonacci term deliberately stays below the sum of its two predecessors; the
values it "refuses to become," namely `A(n+1) + A(n)`, simplify to the shifted squares
`n² + 1`. This shadow set should have natural density zero, contain no long arithmetic
progressions beyond an initial segment, and have a counting function asymptotic to
`√(2m)`.

The key insight is that the shadow a sequence casts by avoidance inherits the growth
order of the sequence itself, so avoidance can never produce a dense set — the very act
of dodging addition forces the dodged values to be sparse. Why now? The exact quadratic
closed form makes the shadow an explicit shifted-square set, converting vague density
claims into concrete, classical questions about squares.

## 4. Residue coverage governed by quadratic residues

Because membership reduces to `m − 1` being triangular, the residues the anti-Fibonacci
sequence can occupy modulo a fixed `q` are exactly the values of `1 + j(j+1)/2`.
Conjecture: the number of residues attained modulo `q` is multiplicative in `q`, and
every residue class is hit only for a very restricted family of `q` (essentially
powers of two times tightly controlled squarefree parts); for all other `q` the
sequence permanently avoids some residues.

The key insight is that a purely additive construction imprints a purely
multiplicative constraint on which residue classes are reachable, linking a greedy
combinatorial rule to the classical theory of quadratic residues. Why now? The clean
triangular-number membership test exposes the residue image as a single quadratic map
modulo `q`, a directly computable object ready for Gauss-sum techniques.

concept.title: Escher Staircases in Algebra: Infinite Ascending Chains That Loop Back
concept.concept_description: An Escher staircase is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... that nevertheless has I_1 as an element of the infinite intersection. This seems impossible — how can an infinite ascending chain loop back to the beginning? But in the ring of integer-valued polynomials Int(Z), the chain I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z} is strictly ascending (I_n strictly contained in I_{n+1}) yet the intersection of all I_n is {0}, which contains the zero polynomial that is also in I_1. Conjecture: Every non-Noetherian ring contains an Escher staircase, and the 'height' of the Escher effect (measured by the Krull dimension gap) is a new ring invariant. For Int(Z), the Escher height is infinite (the chain never stabilizes). For Z[x_1, x_2, ...], the Escher height equals the number of variables. For the p-adic integers Z_p, there is NO Escher staircase (Z_p is a DVR, hence Noetherian). Test: prove that Int(Z) has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Prove that k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n. Compute the Escher height for the ring of all algebraic integers. Impact: a new invariant for non-Noetherian rings that measures how far a ring is from being Noetherian — the algebraic equivalent of Escher's impossible architecture.

# Escher Height, part III: how the staircase transfers between rings

This file extends `Algebra.EscherStaircase` (the definition `Escher.EscherStaircase`
and the ACC characterisation `Escher.escherStaircase_iff_not_isNoetherianRing`) with
the *structural* behaviour of Escher staircases under the three basic ring
operations: taking a finite product, adjoining a single variable, and passing to an
overring.  The point of view is that "admits an Escher staircase" is a ring
*invariant* (it is exactly non-Noetherianity), so it should have clean functorial
transfer laws — and the surprises come from where those laws *fail*.

## Main results

* `Escher.escherStaircase_prod_iff` :
    `EscherStaircase (R × S) ↔ EscherStaircase R ∨ EscherStaircase S`.
    The impossible staircase is a **local-to-global** obstruction: a finite product
    has one iff some factor does.
* `Escher.escherStaircase_polynomial_iff` :
    `EscherStaircase R[X] ↔ EscherStaircase R`.
    Adjoining a *single* variable is **neutral**: it neither creates nor destroys the

An *Escher staircase* is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals that
nevertheless bottoms out — its infimum is its own first rung. Such a chain exists in a
commutative ring exactly when the ring fails the ascending chain condition. This cycle
established that the phenomenon transfers cleanly along surjections (finite products
and single-variable extensions), yet can be *created* by shrinking to a subring: a
non-Noetherian domain lives inside its fraction field, a ring in which the staircase

ideals that can be threaded strictly between consecutive rungs of a grounded ascending
chain (one whose infimum is its bottom rung). Then a polynomial ring in finitely many

# Computational Evidence — Escher Staircases and their transfer laws

An *Escher staircase* in a commutative ring `R` is an infinite strictly ascending
chain of ideals `I₀ ⊊ I₁ ⊊ I₂ ⊊ ⋯`. This cycle studied how the existence of such a
chain transfers between rings.

## 1. Small-case sanity checks

### The concrete product staircase `ℕ → ℤ` (sibling file)
`Sₙ = {f | ∀ k ≥ n, f k = 0}`.
- `S₀ = {0}`, `S₁ = {f | f k = 0 for k ≥ 1}`, `S₂ = …`.
- Strictness witness: `Pi.single n 1 ∈ S_{n+1} \ Sₙ`.
- `⨅ₙ Sₙ = S₀ = {0}` — the chain "loops back" to its bottom rung.

### The variable staircase `k[x₀, x₁, …]`
`Vₙ = ⟨x₀, …, x_{n-1}⟩`. Strictness: `xₙ ∈ V_{n+1} \ Vₙ`, detected by the
endomorphism sending `x_i ↦ 0` (i < n) and fixing the rest. `V₀ = ⊥`.

## 2. Transfer-law spot checks

| Operation                | Prediction                              | Check |
|--------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-------|
| Product `R × S`          | staircase iff a factor has one          | `R = ℚ[x₀,x₁,…]` (yes), `S = ℚ` (no) ⇒ `R × S` yes ✓ |
| Single variable `R[X]`   | staircase iff `R` has one               | `ℚ[X]` (no, PID) ; `ℚ[x₀,x₁,…][X] ≅ ℚ[x₀,x₁,…,x_∞]` still yes ✓ |
| Overring (fraction field)| **not** inherited by subrings           | `ℚ[x₀,x₁,…]` (yes) ↪ `Frac(…)` a field (no) ✓ |

The product law and the single-variable law both follow from the fact that
non-Noetherianity is inherited by any ring that *surjects onto* a non-Noetherian one
(`R × S ↠ R`, `R[X] ↠ R` via evaluation at 0), together with the Hilbert basis
theorem for the reverse polynomial direction.

## 3. Counterexample hunt: is "Escher height monotone under subrings"?

Naively one might expect a subring to be "closer to Noetherian" than its overring.
**FALSE.** The domain `ℚ[x₀, x₁, x₂, …]` is non-Noetherian (infinite variable
staircase) yet embeds into its fraction field, which — being a field — is Noetherian
and has **no** staircase at all. So a subring can be strictly *further* from
Noetherian than the ring containing it. This is the "impossible architecture": the
staircase visible downstairs vanishes upstairs.

## 4. Correction to the original informal chain

The proposed chain `Iₙ = {f ∈ Int(ℤ) : f(ℤ) ⊆ 2ⁿℤ}` is **descending**, not ascending
(`2^{n+1}ℤ ⊆ 2ⁿℤ`), so it is not an Escher staircase as stated. The honest
infinite-height witnesses are the variable chain `⟨x₀⟩ ⊊ ⟨x₀,x₁⟩ ⊊ ⋯` and the
tail-support chain in `ℕ → ℤ`, both of which are genuinely ascending and loop back to
`⊥`.

## 5. OEIS

No integer sequence is central to this cycle (the objects are ideal chains, not
counting sequences), so no OEIS lookup applies.

# Future Directions: Escher Staircases and the Geometry of Non-Noetherian Rings

An *Escher staircase* is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals that
nevertheless bottoms out — its infimum is its own first rung. Such a chain exists in a
commutative ring exactly when the ring fails the ascending chain condition. This cycle
established that the phenomenon transfers cleanly along surjections (finite products
and single-variable extensions), yet can be *created* by shrinking to a subring: a
non-Noetherian domain lives inside its fraction field, a ring in which the staircase
has vanished entirely. The following conjectures push on that tension.

## 1. A genuine numerical height for the Escher effect

**Conjecture.** Attach to each ring an *Escher height*: the longest chain of prime
ideals that can be threaded strictly between consecutive rungs of a grounded ascending
chain (one whose infimum is its bottom rung). Then a polynomial ring in finitely many
variables has height zero, a polynomial ring in infinitely many variables has infinite
height, and the ring of integer-valued polynomials has height equal to its Krull
dimension, two.

The key insight is that the vague notion of a "dimension gap" between the top and
bottom of an impossible staircase becomes a precise invariant only when each rung is
tied to a chain of primes living strictly inside the step to the next rung; the
staircase then measures dimension, not just length.

Why now? The transfer laws established this cycle show that mere existence of a
staircase is too coarse to distinguish rings — products, single variables, and even
some subrings all preserve or manufacture it. A quantitative refinement is the natural
next demand, and the prime-sandwich formulation is the first version that survives the
transfer laws intact.

## 2. The staircase inside the algebraic integers

**Conjecture.** The ring of all algebraic integers admits an explicit Escher staircase
built from successive dyadic roots of two — the radicals generated by the square root,
fourth root, eighth root, and so on — whose infimum is the zero ideal, and its Escher
height is exactly one.

The key insight is that passing to all algebraic integers makes the underlying value
group infinitely divisible, and infinite divisibility is precisely the engine that
produces an endless ascending chain of ideals that still collapses to zero at the
bottom.

Why now? We already understand the infinite-height polynomial example and the
height-zero Noetherian examples; the algebraic integers are the canonical
one-dimensional non-Noetherian ring and would supply the first genuinely intermediate,
arithmetically meaningful value of the height.

## 3. Where does a staircase collapse?

**Conjecture.** For the polynomial ring in countably many variables, the variable
staircase survives every enlargement obtained by inverting finitely many nonzero
elements but disappears the moment infinitely many are inverted; the family of
overrings in which it survives is organized exactly like the cofinite subsets of the
variable set.

The key insight is that a staircase collapses precisely when the enlargement turns
cofinitely many of its rung-generators into units, so the survival question is not
analytic but combinatorial — a question about which generators have been made
invertible.

Why now? This cycle showed a staircase can vanish entirely on passing from a ring to
its fraction field. The next question is *when* along the way it dies, and localization
gives a controllable one-parameter family of intermediate rings in which to watch the
collapse happen.

## 4. Two independent heights, ascending and descending

**Conjecture.** Mirroring the ascending staircase, define a descending Escher
staircase as an infinite strictly descending chain of ideals whose supremum is its top
rung; a ring avoids all of these exactly when it satisfies the descending chain
condition. A ring then admits both kinds of staircase precisely when it is neither
Noetherian nor Artinian, and the ascending and descending heights are independent — any
prescribed pair of values can be realized simultaneously.

The key insight is that failure of the ascending and descending chain conditions are
logically orthogonal, so the two heights can be dialed independently and then combined
by a simple product construction, since a finite product carries a staircase exactly
when one of its factors does.

Why now? The product transfer law proved this cycle is exactly the gluing tool needed
to realize prescribed pairs of invariants, making the independence conjecture testable
by explicit construction rather than abstract existence.

## 5. Staircases in modules, and the reach of finite generation

**Conjecture.** A finitely generated module over a commutative ring contains an
infinite strictly ascending chain of submodules if and only if the base ring itself is
non-Noetherian, so the module-level illusion is entirely governed by the ring. By
contrast, the free module on countably many generators always contains such a chain,
whatever the base ring.

The key insight is that finite generation transports the ascending chain condition
faithfully back and forth between a module and its base ring, which pins the module's
staircase to the ring exactly in the finitely generated case and cuts the tie
completely otherwise.

Why now? The single-variable transfer law of this cycle already rests on reading
Noetherianity through surjections; extending that reasoning from rings to their modules
is the immediate generalization, and it isolates finite generation as the precise
hypothesis under which the ring controls its modules.
